title: How walks work

orient.question: What happens between Claude finishing research and you understanding it?
orient.answer: Claude sends a walk, a toast appears, you step through it and keep the recap.

example.name: Waivers TRD
example.line: Claude has just finished reading the delinquency waivers TRD for dvla.

steps.name: Arrives
steps.takeaway: A walk arrives as a corner toast, never a tab.
steps.body_html: When Claude finishes, it sends the walk to easel. easel files it under the project it came from and a small toast slides into the top-right corner.
steps.picture_html:
$ npm run test
you keep typing here
New walkdvla · Waivers TRD
steps.example_html: You are mid-command in the terminal. The Waivers TRD toast appears; your next keystroke still lands in the terminal.
steps.slower_html: Nothing opens and nothing steals your keyboard. The toast stays for 8 seconds. If three walks arrive at once they stack; a fourth becomes "+1 more".
steps.why_html: A tab you have to find is the reason easel felt unnatural. A toast tells you something is ready without breaking what you are doing.

steps.name: Orient
steps.takeaway: You see the answer and the size before you start.
steps.body_html: Opening a walk lands on Orient: the question it answers, the answer in one line, how long it takes, and a map of its parts.
steps.picture_html:
1line answer
7steps
5 minto walk
steps.example_html: Waivers TRD opens on: "A waiver is drafted by an officer, approved by a supervisor, then written to the ledger." 6 steps, about 6 minutes.
steps.slower_html: You know the destination before the first step. If the one-line answer is all you needed, you can stop there.
steps.why_html: Not knowing where to start is the first thing that costs you time. The size and the map answer "how big is this and what matters" up front.

steps.name: Pick depth
steps.takeaway: You choose which parts to go deep on.
steps.body_html: The map comes with a suggested path already ticked. Untick what you already know; those parts stay at their one-line takeaway.
steps.picture_html:
• Arrives
  • Orient
  • Pick depth
  • One step
  • Ask
  • Check
  • Keep
steps.example_html: You already know how the ledger works, so you untick Ledger write. The walk drops from 6 steps to 5.
steps.slower_html: Taking the suggested path is one key. Picking is optional, never required.
steps.why_html: Walking parts you already know is where focus drains. Skipping them keeps the walk short enough to finish.

steps.name: One step
steps.takeaway: One idea per step, with Slower and Why ready.
steps.body_html: Each step holds one idea: a takeaway line, a picture, and the running example applied to it. Slower and Why are written in advance, so they open instantly.
steps.picture_html:
ButtonWhat happensWaits on Claude?
Got itNext stepNo
SlowerPlainer version with the exampleNo
Why?The reason behind this stepNo
AskYour own question answeredYes, about 20 s
steps.example_html: The Waivers step "Supervisor approves" shows a swimlane with one waiver moving from officer to supervisor.
steps.slower_html: If a step does not land, press S. You get the same idea in plainer words with the example worked through.
steps.why_html: One idea per step means you can stop anywhere and resume exactly there, which is what keeps focus from dropping midway.

steps.name: Ask
steps.takeaway: Ask gets a fresh answer from the walk's own sources.
steps.body_html: Ask starts a fresh, read-only Claude call in the project folder with the walk and your question. The answer is inserted as a new step right after the one you were on.
steps.picture_html:
1. You ask"Can a supervisor approve their own waiver?"
  2. Claude readswalk sources + project files, read-only
  3. New stepinserted after this one, saved
steps.example_html: On the approval step you ask whether a supervisor can approve their own waiver. About 20 seconds later a new step answers it, citing the TRD.
steps.slower_html: The session that made the walk can be closed. Ask does not need it.
steps.why_html: Your follow-up question is usually the thing that makes an idea stick. Answering it inside the walk keeps you in one place.

steps.name: Check
steps.takeaway: Saying it back shows you whether it stuck.
steps.body_html: At the end, up to three prompts. You type a one-line answer, the expected answer appears beside it, and you mark it right or not.
steps.picture_html:
You wrote

Supervisor signs it off

Expected

A supervisor approves it before the ledger is written
steps.example_html: "Who approves a waiver?" You write "supervisor". The expected answer agrees; you mark it right.
steps.slower_html: Check is optional. Skipping it still saves the recap.
steps.why_html: Reading something is not the same as being able to say it. Trying to recall it is what makes it stay.

steps.name: Keep
steps.takeaway: Recap and actions stay with the project.
steps.body_html: Finishing a walk saves its recap lines and action items to the project's Keep page. Home shows every project and where you stopped in each.
steps.picture_html:
dvla1 waiting · 1 in progress
easel2 waiting
graall done
steps.example_html: Next week, dvla's Keep page still has "Supervisor approves before the ledger write" and the action "Read the waiver API contract".
steps.slower_html: Walks belong to projects, not to Claude sessions, so closing a session never loses one.
steps.why_html: Juggling projects is easier when each one remembers what you learned and what you still owe it.

check.prompt: Where does a new walk show up first?
check.expected: A small toast in the top-right corner

check.prompt: Does Ask need the Claude session that made the walk?
check.expected: No, it starts a fresh read-only call

recap: A walk arrives as a toast and never takes your keyboard.
Orient gives the answer and the size first.
Each step is one idea, with Slower and Why ready.
Ask answers from the walk's sources, even after the session closes.
Recaps and actions stay with the project.
